title: Best of Un/filmed: Short Documentaries from Russian Speaking Filmmakers | Additional Films and Guests
location: IU Cinema,1213 East 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA
description:
Un/Filmed is an international documentary film development project and a regular partner with the Byrnes Institute at IU focused on preserving the tradition of independent documentary filmmaking among Russian-speakers, and to provide competitive workshops for participants with the opportunity to create films reflecting on pressing social issues. This program is showcasing the top six films of the 2024-2025 cohort with subtitles presented in English.

Like Mother, Like Daughter (dir. Sofia Sedlova, 2025, Russia and France): Yana—who’s unexpectedly pregnant—and her daughter Liza await their papers in a Paris suburb. Uncertainty sparks personal crises for Yana and forces Liza to grow up too fast. Their roles reverse in this small family, but together they’ll face the challenges ahead. [7 min; Russian and French with English subtitles]

We're Fine (dir. Daria Yurishcheva, 2025, Russia and France): Two old acquaintances share an apartment in Marseille by force of circumstances. The talkative Ukrainian Andrii is forced to take care of the gloomy Russian Filipp. The migrant's instability will not make Andrii lose his optimism. [16 min; Russian and French with English subtitles]

She Became a Pillar of Salt (dir. Xenia Vasilkova, 2025, Russia): A Russian filmmaker and her Ukrainian friend rebuild their lives in Armenia after fleeing their homelands. As war draws all apart, we uncover quiet echoes between them. [15 min; Russian with English subtitles]

Uneasy Living (dir. Nikita Nadezhdin, 2025, Russia): A Russian, staunchly against war, flees to Georgia after protest detentions, battling depression and scorn from traditional society while scavenging in dumpsters and aiding stray cats. Through quiet acts of kindness, he searches for life's meaning. This intimate documentary explores hope, humanity, and defiance against outdated norms. [15 min; Russian with English subtitles]

Kozlov Mitya, 81+ (dir. Yulia Ruzmanova, 2025, Russia): What matters most in relationships in your 80s: a hug, a sack of potatoes, a kind word, or simply having someone to spend New Year’s Eve with? This is a road trip with Mitya Kozlov and his dog as he visits his girlfriends, searching for an answer to this question. [17 min; Russian with English subtitles]

Memory is Me? (dir. Vlada Lodesk, 2025, Russia): To get acquainted with her deceased dad, whom she never met, a filmmaker follows the traces of him in her mother’s memories and the artifacts that are left behind. Along the way, she writes letters to her father—letters that cannot be sent. [15 min; Russian with English subtitles]

title: Death Cafe
location: Morgenstern Books & Cafe, 849 South Auto Mall Road, Bloomington
description:
A Death Cafe is a group-directed discussion of death with no agenda, ideology, objectives, or themes. It is a discussion group rather than grief support or counseling session. Death Cafes have spread quickly around the world. Over 16,500 Death Cafes are held in 85 countries. It is all volunteer-run.
The monthly Death Cafe at Morgenstern Books is run by co-hosts Rick Clayton and Casey Stover. Rick Clayton is a hospice chaplain, end-of life doula, and musician who enjoys playing harp, cello, and guitar for his clients. Casey Stover is a Certified Family Life Educator whose professional work often exists adjacent to death and grief, shaping her belief in the importance of accessible spaces to normalize honest conversation and community care.
You can find our Death Cafe at the back corner of the bookstore, near the restrooms, on the last Tuesday of every month at 7 pm.

title: Victoria Popritkin, soprano; Shuichi Umeyama, piano
description: Repertoire  Wolf: Selections from "Goethe-Lieder" (1888)Rachmaninoff: Selections from "Études-tableaux, Op. 33" (1911)Rachmaninoff: Six Romances, Op. 38 (1916)About the Faculty ArtistShuichi Umeyama is assistant professor of music and an opera coach at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. A sought-out collaborator by internationally prominent vocalists, pianist Umeyama is a highly seasoned concert performer. Equally at ease as a soloist and accompanist, he commands a vast repertoire in both vocal and instrumental literature. He has performed piano concertos by Brahms, Beethoven, Chopin, and Rachmaninoff, among others, and his recitals have been broadcast on Japan National Broadcasting (NHK). In the United States, Umeyama has served as coach or accompanist for San Francisco Opera, Houston Grand Opera, Santa Fe Opera, Opera Theatre of Saint Louis, Opera North, Indianapolis Opera, and others. He has been an official accompanist for the Metropolitan Opera National Laffont Competition for over 30 years. As a musical coach, he has participated in numerous operatic world premieres, including Our Town (Rorem), Jeppe (Sandstrom), Vincent (Rands), The Tale of Lady Thị Kính, What the Horse Eats (Phan), Anne Frank (Ran), Tevye's Daughters (Weiser), and The Amazing Adventures of Kavalier and Clay (Bates). In 2017, Umeyama taught voice students at Aichi University of the Arts in Japan as a resident artist. He earned Bachelor of Music and Master of Music degrees from Tokyo National University of Fine Arts and Music.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
location: LILLY LIBRARY - Room Number: Ball Room
description: "Myths are the world’s dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

title: Total African Cinema Exhibit
location: Black Film Center and Archive, 1320 E. 10th Street, Wells Library 044, Bloomington, IN, 47405 - Room Number: Exhibit/Reception Area
description: Donated by the Vieyra family in June 2021, the exhibition showcases highlights from The Paulin S. Vieyra Collection. The display case features intimate and rare items, including family portraits, Vieyra's typewriter, and a 16mm reel of Môl (1966). Five original collages by graphic designer Pouya Jahanshahi are at the center of the exhibition. Jahanshahi collaborated with Project Archivist Jason Byrne, who shaped the exhibition's themes and selected archival content. Student workers Sarah Petras, Thomas Pigott, Cree Prince, and Kudzai Zinyemba supported the project by helping process and research the materials.  The TOTAL AFRICAN CINEMA exhibit is on view in the BFCA reception area now through May 31, 2026!

Originally trained in plant sciences, she transitioned to art to explore texture, color, and material more deeply, using a mix of fibers and found objects to create richly layered, tactile pieces inspired by both the natural world and personal experience.

This exhibition will be on display from Wednesday, April 1-Saturday, April 25! Don't forget to stop by on Friday, April 3 from 5-8 pm for the artist reception for this month's Gallery Walk. Come to meet with the artist, connect with the arts community, and enjoy light refreshments.

title: Meet-The-Author: Medinay Bawudun, Rise Up My Uyghurs
description: Medinay Bawudun has spent 26 years away from her homeland, yet she continues to stand proudly for Uyghur culture. Through her poetry and music, she shares the stories, struggles, and resilient spirit of her people with audiences around the world. For 17 years, she worked as a journalist at Ürümqi TV and Radio Free Asia, exploring themes of identity, homeand social awareness, and her dual perspective as both journalist and poet allows her to reflect the Uyghur experience with honesty, sensitivity, and depth. Collaborating with artists across Central Asia and creating powerful songs like "Rise Up My Uyghurs" and "The Way Back Home", Bawudun has become a heartfelt and inspiring voice for the Uyghur diaspora. As the founder of the Uyghur Culture Heritage Project, she tirelessly works to preserve and share Uyghur traditions, using her poetry and music to build a bridge that invites listeners to feel, connect, and celebrate the enduring spirit of Uyghur culture.   Co-sponsored by Bloomington's own Marco & Polo Uyghur and Eurasian restaurant, in consortium with the Center for the Languages of the Central Asian Region.

title: The Spirit, Shade and Shape of Sasanian Women and Its Impact on Female Images along the Silk Road - a Lecture by Dr. Chen Su
description: By synthesizing archaeological remains with textual evidence, this lecture explores the multifaceted roles and images of Sasanian women through the lens of late antique Persian culture. Under the influence of Zoroastrian dualism, the perception of women in ancient Iran was divided into two categories—the "good" and the "evil"—a paradox that deeply informed their figures in religious writing, secular literature, and artistic presentations. This talk will highlight the significant presence of female iconography across various materials, including coins, seals, metalwork, and rock reliefs, tracing how these vibrant artistic depictions traveled along the Silk Road into Central and East Asia. Furthermore, the lecture will examine how specific Sasanian visual motifs and formalized patterns left a lasting imprint on the portrayal of women within the Buddhist and secular art of medieval China and Central Asia.  Dr. Su Chen is a lecturer at Inner Mongolia University and currently a visiting scholar at the IAUNRC. She received her Ph.D. from Peking University in 2023, after a year of doctoral exchange studies at CEUS in 2020. Her research focuses on Iranian history and Sino-Iran cultural exchange along the Silk Road, drawing primarily on Middle Persian and Classical Persian historical sources. She has published papers on topics including the urban history of the Ilkhanate, Sasanian social history, and Persian historiography. Meeting URL: https://iu.zoom.us/j/85266676542

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
location: LILLY LIBRARY - Room Number: Ball Room
description: "Myths are the world’s dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

description:
Artists for Climate Awareness invites people of all ages to experience “Art as Inquiry,” a juried climate‑art exhibition on view April 2–29 at the Pillar Arts Alliance Center in Bloomington, IN and online. Featuring 2‑D and 3‑D works from artists across several states, this Earth Month exhibition explores urgent climate and environmental issues through creative expression and community engagement.

Art, especially, can turn scientific knowledge into experiences that resonate emotionally—offering insights that facts and figures alone can’t always reach. When these perspectives come together, they open up fresh ways of seeing and help people connect more deeply with complex ideas. “Art as Inquiry” invites visitors to encounter climate research, ecological change, and environmental justice through the lens of artistic imagination.

Beginning April 19, artwork from the Climate Co‑lab \(Brushes for a Better Planet\) joins the exhibition, displayed alongside the Art as Inquiry works.

Earth Month Events \(Free; Public Invited\):

April 12, 2–3 pm – Nature Walk, a musical and narrative performance led by IU Jacobs School of Music student Thejas Mirle and four composers, with narration by Distinguished IU Biology Professor Roger Hangarter.

April 12, 3–5 pm – Reception for the member climate‑art exhibition; prizes awarded. 🌱

April 19, 3–6 pm – Climate Co‑lab Reception \+ Nature Walk performance; brief introductions of artists and partners.

title: "Meet the Barbarians" Film Screening
location: HERMAN B WELLS LIBRARY - Room Number: Screening Room
description: Join us at the Wells Library screening room to watch French film Meet the Barbarians, part of the HLS Movie Night series.  When a French village accidentally welcomes the "wrong" refugee family, their assumptions get turned upside down. Director Julie Delpy's warm, funny dramedy asks who the real barbarians are when fear meets humanity.  This film was the summer 2024 box office hit in Europe. The town council of Paimpont, a small village in Brittany, has unanimously voted in favor of welcoming a family of Ukrainian refugees. However, the refugees who turn up aren't Ukrainian but Syrian, and some of the locals are not very pleased with their new neighbors. Yet the Fayad family avoids all the clichés the French villagers may have expected. So much so that, they leave one wondering: who in this little village are the true 'barbarians'? A film that gives you laughs, tears, cheers, and a good dose of Breton Sun.   Watch a trailer for the film here. (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6MBI076ZRU8)

Explore colorful coral reefs, playful fish, and fantastical sea creatures — all meticulously hand-knit and crocheted.  Pause to reflect on the delicate balance between human wellbeing and the vitality of our oceans.  Chat with a Museum Guide to deepen your understanding.  Create Your Own Sea CreatureEnjoy a hands-on activity in the gallery.  No prior experience is needed — a volunteer can guide you step by step.  Choose from a fish, octopus, lobster, sea urchin, or crab.  All supplies are provided, so you can dive right in!  Why Visit? This exhibition is more than art — it's a living conversation about beauty, fragility, and our shared responsibility to protect the ocean. Whether you're an art lover, a family looking for a creative activity, or simply curious, Vital Ecosystems offers a memorable experience for all ages.

Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
location: LILLY LIBRARY - Room Number: Ball Room
description: "Myths are the world’s dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

title: "Art as Inquiry," A Gallery Show
description:

Featuring 2‑D and 3‑D works from artists across several states, this Earth Month exhibition explores urgent climate and environmental issues through creative expression and community engagement.

Art, especially, can turn scientific knowledge into experiences that resonate emotionally—offering insights that facts and figures alone can’t always reach. When these perspectives come together, they open up fresh ways of seeing and help people connect more deeply with complex ideas. “Art as Inquiry” invites visitors to encounter climate research, ecological change, and environmental justice through the lens of artistic imagination.

title: 21JPSI/EASC: "The Role of Dialect in Contemporary Japanese Society"(Prof. Jae Takeuchi; IU)
location: GLOBAL & INTERNATIONAL STUDIES BUILDING - Room Number: 1112
description: Talk abstract: Japanese dialects continue to be used in regions across Japan, despite the promotion of Standard Japanese through education and media. Drawing on examples from Ehime Prefecture, this presentation will discuss how Japanese dialects are evolving and consider what they contribute to the linguistic landscape of contemporary Japan.Jae DiBello Takeuchi is Associate Professor of Japanese in the Department of East Asian Languages and Cultures at Indiana University. Dr. Takeuchi conducts research in Japanese sociolinguistics and applied linguistics, second language acquisition, and foreign language pedagogy. Her research focuses on the experiences of Japanese second language speakers who are long-term residents of Japan. She is particularly interested in how they navigate Japanese speech styles, such as dialects and keigo, which they encounter in local communities, workplaces, and leisure activities. At Indiana University, Dr. Takeuchi teaches courses in Japanese language and sociolinguistics. Before coming to Indiana, she taught Japanese at Clemson University and served as the director of the Languages and International Business program.  Dr. Takeuchi's 2023 book Language Ideologies and L2 Speaker Legitimacy: Native Speaker Bias in Japan examines native speaker bias and L2 speaker legitimacy. Her recent projects focus on linguistic microaggression and consider how speaker identity and markers such as accent impact L2 speakers' acceptance in Japanese communities.

title: ACES Horizon Talk: Dr. Charlotte D'Evelyn, "The Choor Fiddle and Sonic Imagination of the Past in Inner Mongolia, China"
description: Musical practices of the Mongol people have become increasingly well known around the world, particularly Mongolian throat-singing and the two-string horsehead fiddle, morin khuur. Much less is known about treasured local fiddle forms in Inner Asia, such as the ikel from Western Mongolia and the choor from Eastern Inner Mongolia, China. In this talk, Professor D'Evelyn explores the important role that the choor fiddle has played in Inner Mongolia, both as part of storytelling ritual in the past and as part of a cultural revival in the present.    Due to historical ruptures and a growing emphasis on staged performance, the choor fiddle was largely neglected and transmitted by only a small number of practitioners during the mid-twentieth century. Beginning in the early 2000s, however, renewed interest in the instrument led many young people to view the choor as a sonic link to a tradition that predates the establishment of the People's Republic of China. Drawing on theories of revival (Bithell and Hill 2013) and scholarship on intangible cultural heritage in China (Tang 2021; Wong 2019; Wilcox 2018; Maags and Svensson 2018), this talk examines how the choor functions as a sonic resource for bringing the past into the present—paradoxically operating both as a uniquely local Eastern Mongolian tradition and as a region-wide sonic emblem of Inner Mongolia.      Charlotte D'Evelyn (PhD, University of Hawai'i at Mānoa, 2013) is an ethnomusicologist who has spent over a decade studying music and the politics of ethnicity in Inner Mongolia, China. Her career in ethnomusicology began in 2002 when she first traveled to China for language exchange and began studying the Chinese erhu (two-string fiddle). Her interest in this instrument developed into a broader focus on spike fiddles and the music cultures of the Silk Road regions. Her research on the Mongolian morin khuur (horsehead fiddle) led her to Inner Mongolia, where she regularly conducts fieldwork on fiddles and vocal traditions along the China–Mongolia border. At Skidmore College, she teaches interdisciplinary courses such as Thinking About Music, Cross-Cultural Listening, and Global Pop, and directs both the Chinese Ensemble and the Mongolia Ensemble. title: REEI Colloquium: "Ukraine's Alleged 'East-West' Domestic Divide: Why Has the Country Survived 2014 and 2022?" with Petro Kuzyk
location: GLOBAL & INTERNATIONAL STUDIES BUILDING - Room Number: 4067
description: Since gaining independence in 1991, Ukraine has often been regarded as a hopelessly divided society and a failing polity. However, this sticky image of Ukraine does not match the fact that the country has been able to resist both Russia's limited military and hybrid attack in 2014 and full-scale aggression in 2022. In this presentation, Dr. Kuzyk will address the issue of deluded and manipulated interpretations of Ukrainian domestic 'east-west' differences. He will argue that the alleged 'east-west' split is overstated, unstable, receding over time, and shaped by foreign misconceptions about Ukraine's societal differences as much as by internal political disputes and conflicts.  Petro Kuzyk is an Associate Professor of the International Relations Department at Ivan Franko National University of Lviv (Ukraine). His recent research has focused on Ukraine's 'east-west' cleavage and its international misinterpretations, as well as the representation of the country's wartime diplomatic efforts in domestic public discourse. During the 2025-26 academic year, Petro Kuzyk is a Fulbright Visiting Professor at the Byrnes Institute of Indiana University-Bloomington.

title: Author event with Sven Becker
location: Morgenstern Books & Cafe, 849 South Auto Mall Road, Bloomington
description:
Author and Harvard professor Sven Beckert, will be discussing his latest book, Capitalism: A Global History.
ABOUT THE BOOK:
No other phenomenon has shaped human history as decisively as capitalism. It structures how we live and work, how we think about ourselves and others, how we organize our politics.  Capitalism, argues Beckert, was born global.  By chronicling capitalism’s global history, Beckert exposes the reality of the system that now seems simply “natural.” Sven Beckert doesn’t merely tote up capitalism’s debits and credits. He shows us how to look through and beyond it to imagine a different and larger world.

Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
location: LILLY LIBRARY - Room Number: Ball Room
description: "Myths are the world’s dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

title: Fire on the Landscape with Sam Shoaf
location: The Laura Hare Nature Preserve at Downey Hill
description: The whippoorwill, a species of concern here in Indiana, has found safe refuge in the recently burned areas of Downey Hill, but why? Join us for a guided hike through the Laura Hare Nature Preserve at Downey Hill with Sam Shoaf, Director of Operations and Burn Boss at Eco Logic, LLC, to explore the vital role of fire in Indiana’s ecosystems. Sam will share insights into how prescribed burns are planned and conducted, and how fire helps maintain healthy forests, promote native plant growth, and support wildlife diversity. Participants will walk through areas recently shaped by fire and learn how this natural process contributes to long-term habitat restoration and resilience.

title: "Art as Inquiry," A Gallery Show
description:
Artists for Climate Awareness invites people of all ages to experience “Art as Inquiry,” a juried climate‑art exhibition on view April 2–29 at the Pillar Arts Alliance Center in Bloomington, IN and online. Featuring 2‑D and 3‑D works from artists across several states, this Earth Month exhibition explores urgent climate and environmental issues through creative expression and community engagement.

Art, especially, can turn scientific knowledge into experiences that resonate emotionally—offering insights that facts and figures alone can’t always reach. When these perspectives come together, they open up fresh ways of seeing and help people connect more deeply with complex ideas. “Art as Inquiry” invites visitors to encounter climate research, ecological change, and environmental justice through the lens of artistic imagination.

Beginning April 19, artwork from the Climate Co‑lab \(Brushes for a Better Planet\) joins the exhibition, displayed alongside the Art as Inquiry works.

Earth Month Events \(Free; Public Invited\):

April 12, 2–3 pm – Nature Walk, a musical and narrative performance led by IU Jacobs School of Music student Thejas Mirle and four composers, with narration by Distinguished IU Biology Professor Roger Hangarter.

April 12, 3–5 pm – Reception for the member climate‑art exhibition; prizes awarded. 🌱

April 19, 3–6 pm – Climate Co‑lab Reception \+ Nature Walk performance; brief introductions of artists and partners.

Gallery Hours: • Thu–Sat: 2–8 pm • Sun: 12–6 pm Pillar Arts Alliance Center, College Mall, Bloomington. Free admission.

Mozart: Symphony No. 41 in C Major, K.551 ("Jupiter")Horn soloist to be announced  About the ConductorArthur Fagen is professor of music in orchestral conducting and cochair of the Department of Orchestral Conducting at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music, where he has been on faculty since 2008. Additionally, he has been music director of The Atlanta Opera since 2010. Fagen has conducted opera productions at the world's most prestigious opera houses and music festivals. From 1998 to 2001, he was invited regularly as guest conductor at the Vienna State Opera. On the concert podium, he has appeared with numerous internationally known orchestras. Fagen has an opera repertory of more than 100 works. He has served as principal conductor in Kassel and Brunswick, as chief conductor of the Flanders Opera of Antwerp and Ghent, as music director of the Queens Symphony Orchestra, and as a member of the conducting staff of Lyric Opera of Chicago. From 2002 to 2007, he was music director of the Dortmund Philharmonic Orchestra and the Dortmund Opera. He and the Dortmund Philharmonic were invited to the Concertgebouw in Amsterdam and the Palais de Beaux Arts in Brussels as well as to Salzburg, Beijing, and Shanghai. Fagen conducted a new production of Turandot at the Atlanta Opera in 2007, opening the season and inaugurating the new opera house, the Cobb Energy Performing Arts Center. He was first-prize winner of the Baltimore Symphony Orchestra Conductors' Competition as well as a prizewinner of the Gino Marinuzzi International Conductors' Competition in Italy. Fagen has recorded for BMG, Bayerischer Rundfunk, SFB, and WDR Cologne. He records regularly for Naxos, for which he has completed the six symphonies of Bohuslav Martinů. His Naxos recording of Martinů's piano concertos was awarded an Editor's Choice award in the March 2010 issue of Gramophone magazine.

title: Traveling University – Vaccines: Over 200 Years of Saving Lives, but Are We Ready for the Next Pandemic?
location: Morgan County Public Library - Main Branch, 110 South Jefferson Street, Martinsville
description: Vaccines have been saving lives for over 200 years, but recent decisions by the current administration have put millions at risk for known diseases as well as possible future pandemics. In this presentation, IU Emerita Professor of Biology, Patricia Foster, will briefly review what vaccines are, how they protect against infections, and how their efficacy and safety are determined. Then she will delve into the science of mRNA vaccines, how they were developed, how effective they were against the COVID pandemic, and why they are our best defense against upcoming pandemics. Please note that this event will be held in Martinsville, IN, at the Morgan County Public Library.

title: Double Exposure 2026 | IU Cinema
location: IU Cinema,1213 East 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47406, USA
description:
Presenting original student work, Double Exposure is an innovative and collaborative program made possible through a partnership which brings together The Media School Cinematic Arts, Jacobs School of Music’s Music Scoring for Visual Media program, and IU Cinema. Each film is made, scored, and sound-designed by Indiana University students and will receive its world-premiere presentation on IU Cinema's big screen.

Any film screened at IU Cinema may contain content that viewers find sensitive or upsetting. Visit our Audience Advisories https://cinema.indiana.edu/plan-visit/audience-advisories.html page to learn more.

Anchors

Director: Rocco Jann | Music: Carson Merical

Anchors is a chaotic, farcical duel for viewership between two insane media personalities. While some films make thoughtful critiques of the current state of our broadcast news landscape, Anchors opts for a… different approach. Absurd headlines, unhinged media personalities, whacky visuals—Anchors seeks to make fun of the news in order to make sense of it. So, sit back, grab a friend, and strap in tight, because it’s time to watch the news like you’ve never seen it before. (7 min)

Rainbow Night

Director: Catie Stanton | Music: Tianqi Zhang

When Cassandra, a beautiful soul who has lost her way, goes home, she is faced with a choice: to follow in her mother’s footsteps or to be better. This therapeutic film exhibits a combination of anger, resentment, love, loss, but most importantly, hope. Writer and director CM Stanton, composer Tianqi Zhang, and everyone else hope to take you in, transform you, and heal you. Contains suicide and mental health issues. (6 min)

Handlebars

Director: Dylan Dankel | Music: Niki Simerly

Aging out of foster care, Rowan faces the uncertainty of independence with little more than a backpack, a trash bag of clothes, and a frayed photograph of his younger sibling Riley. Fueled by the drive to reconnect, he sets out into the night.

There’s a Cult in these Woods

Director: Nolan Goode | Music: Theo Morris

I’ve come to the conclusion that I can never be content with one specific way of life, or way of thinking. When it comes to these things, I’m too curious of a person, a trait slowly dying from the chokehold that goliaths like organized religion and technology have put us in. That’s a large reason why I made this film. (6 min)

Invocation

Director: Betsy Leija | Music: Sean Giovanetti

Have you ever felt that something was calling to you? That somewhere in the dark, something was waiting, promising to awaken feelings you have never known? In Invocation, Isa is caught in the haunting struggle between her religious past and a mysterious being that calls to her each night, drawing her toward forbidden desire and uneasy serenity. As her longing deepens, Isa must confront whether surrender is damnation or liberation. (5 min)

Euphoric Spit

Director: Blake Schwandt | Music: Donavan Walker

Set in a charged Los Angeles summer, the film follows a young artist’s journey through fleeting sexual encounters that open portals into his unfelt interior world. What begins as bodily exchange becomes a spiritual excavation—an attempt to sense the parts of himself that exist beyond sight. Through fragmented memories, warmth, and ecstatic disorientation, the film maps desire as a path toward wholeness. (5 min)

Devourer

Director: Goodman Murphy-Smith | Music: Tu Gu

A nameless teenager wanders an unfamiliar house infested by a past it cannot forget. Deep in its endless hallways, a door hides many eyes. Devourer is a sleepwalk through a contemporary teenage experience, lost in a landscape of violent videos, alienation, and technology rotting in the shadow of the Information Age. Contains implied violence against a child and brief flashing lights. (6 min)

Game Theory 101

Director: Gracie Runge | Music: Shmuli Myers

Dom and Kevin, two best friends who enjoy hosting legendary game nights in their apartment, are pushed to their breaking point by their acquaintance, Fitz, who constantly crashes out during games. Fitz is a poor sport, and every time he loses a game, he goes “nuclear.” Dom and Kevin propose a challenge to Fitz: he has one last chance at game night before he is banned from game nights forever. (8 min)

Nostalgia is a Liar

Director: Deo Akiode | Music: Donavan Walker

Our actions outlive us, but so will our inactions. We all live with the burden of our regrets and mistakes, but for some of us, we know our time to make amends for them is running short. In this film, we watch a desperate man try valiantly to do so: his journey reflecting themes of loss, memory, and harsh honesty. (8 min)

To This Ocean

Director: Polina Saburova | Music: Camilo Rincón

This is an experimental multilingual audio-visual poem about home and belonging in the context of migration in the ever-changing world. How can you create a home where there isn’t supposed to be one? When you leave, what stays with you of the place that you call home? Is it a smell or a touch or an image or a sound? Who or what is a home? (6 min)

title: E5C4P3: The Music Of Journey
location: Brown County Playhouse, 70 S. Van Buren St, Nashville, IN, 47448, United States
description:
E5C4P3 was formed in June of 1993. From that year through 1999, E5C4P3 traveled nationwide and paid tribute to one of rock history’s most beloved bands, performing for tens of thousands of fans. E5C4P3 is still known today as the original and best Journey tribute band to ever exist. In 1999, E5C4P3 went on hiatus and the world was suddenly filled with multiple Journey tributes trying to fill the void that E5C4P3 left behind. In 2008, E5C4P3 was reformed to recreate the magic of a Journey concert like no one else can. The band covers the music with a note-for-note accuracy that is second to none and performs each show with the high-energy excitement of a real Journey concert as well as visually recreating the essence of early 80’s Journey! Focusing on the “Steve Perry era,” E5C4P3 covers all the hits from “Lights” and “Wheel In The Sky” to “Separate Ways” and “Be Good To Yourself,” including occasional surprises for all the die-hard Journey fans.  For all of the countless fans that have never stopped believing, they’re back!

title: "Art as Inquiry," A Gallery Show
description:
Artists for Climate Awareness invites people of all ages to experience “Art as Inquiry,” a juried climate‑art exhibition on view April 2–29 at the Pillar Arts Alliance Center in Bloomington, IN and online. Featuring 2‑D and 3‑D works from artists across several states, this Earth Month exhibition explores urgent climate and environmental issues through creative expression and community engagement.

Art, especially, can turn scientific knowledge into experiences that resonate emotionally—offering insights that facts and figures alone can’t always reach. When these perspectives come together, they open up fresh ways of seeing and help people connect more deeply with complex ideas. “Art as Inquiry” invites visitors to encounter climate research, ecological change, and environmental justice through the lens of artistic imagination.

Beginning April 19, artwork from the Climate Co‑lab \(Brushes for a Better Planet\) joins the exhibition, displayed alongside the Art as Inquiry works.

Earth Month Events \(Free; Public Invited\):

April 12, 2–3 pm – Nature Walk, a musical and narrative performance led by IU Jacobs School of Music student Thejas Mirle and four composers, with narration by Distinguished IU Biology Professor Roger Hangarter.

April 12, 3–5 pm – Reception for the member climate‑art exhibition; prizes awarded. 🌱

April 19, 3–6 pm – Climate Co‑lab Reception \+ Nature Walk performance; brief introductions of artists and partners.

Gallery Hours: • Thu–Sat: 2–8 pm • Sun: 12–6 pm Pillar Arts Alliance Center, College Mall, Bloomington. Free admission.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
location: LILLY LIBRARY - Room Number: Ball Room
description: "Myths are the world’s dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

title: Spring 2026 Colloquium Series with Carlos Colmenares Gil
description: The Center for Latin American and Caribbean Studies is proud to present the continuation of its Colloquium Series for Spring 2026.  We welcome Dr. Carlos Colmenares Gil as he presents Miguel James and the "Angelitos Negros" of Venezuelan Poetry.  This presentation examines Venezuelan-Trinidadian poet Miguel James' oeuvre as critical of a national project of racial democracy in Venezuela, and of how such a project informs structures of literary reception by limiting them. In a country where both political and cultural discourse frame and construct a Venezuelan identity as a seemingly flexible mestizaje, James' work demands taking a step back from it and articulating these heterogeneous cultural and social elements otherwise. James' seemingly multiculturalist enumerations and mixture of referents move away from a radical critique; instead, they offer a counterpoint where mestizaje as a demagogic identity is displaced in favor of a process of amefricanidade, as theorized by Lélia González, in which blackness is neither monumentalized in an immemorial past, nor dissolved in a postracial present. To understand this transition from one socio-political structure of meaning to another, Stuart Hall's concept of articulation will be key to illuminating James' poetry.    Carlos Colmenares Gil studies the Spanish-Caribbean, continental Caribbean, and Brazil, specifically how the cultural expressions (literature, film, music) from these areas are immersed, or resist to be immersed, in a cosmopolitan logic which translates and creates a simplified structure of critical reception for them. His work engages with a long tradition of Latin American thought as well as continental philosophy, psychoanalysis, and anthropology, examining questions of high and low art, the idea of the popular, the hyper and translocal, and the intellectual life of minoritized subjects. He has published on social theorist Alejandro Moreno and on Afro-Venezuelan music. Currently, he is working on a book project focused on Venezuelan poetry and the critique of interiority; and a long essay centered around Igor Barreto and the destruction and re-composition of the landscape in relation to other Latin American poets. In parallel, he continues to research on Afro-Latin drums and the voices and chants that accompany them.                 The CLACS Spring 2026 Colloquium meets Mondays from February through April, with faculty and guest speakers engaging Latin America and the Caribbean through research on history, culture, language, politics, and the arts. Check the CLACS Calendar (https://events.iu.edu/clacs/) for details.
source: IU Hamilton Lugar School, IU La Casa Latino Cultural Center

title: Tom Walsh Jazz Ensemble
description: About the DirectorTom Walsh is Robert J. Waller Sr. and Robert J. Waller Jr. Professor of Music (saxophone) and chair of the Jazz Studies Department at the Indiana University Jacobs School of Music. An active performer of jazz and classical music, he has presented concerts and workshops in South Africa, China, Brazil, Japan, Germany, Austria, Italy, Croatia, Slovenia, Azerbaijan, Costa Rica, and across the United States. In 2019, his beginning improvisation book Jazz Master Teaches You to Improvise was published by Shanghai Music Publishing House. Recent recordings include The Pandemic Sessions by the IU jazz faculty, Luke Gillespie's Moving Mists, Basically Baker, Vol. 2, with the Buselli-Wallarab Jazz Orchestra (Patois), Mike Hackett's New Point of View (Summit) and two CDs released on the IUMusic label: Holiday Celebration and Sylvia McNair's Romance. Premiere performances include Scott Jones's concert band arrangement of Russell Peck's The Upward Stream, Chris Rutkowski's Concerto for Alto Saxophone and Wind Ensemble, and David Baker's Concerto for Alto Saxophone and Orchestra. His latest solo CD release is Intersections (Arizona University Recordings), featuring Luke Gillespie on piano. Earlier solo CDs include New Life (RIAX) and Shaking the Pumpkin (RIAX). Other releases include the David Baker Concerto with the Czech National Symphony Orchestra on Paul Freeman Introduces David Baker, Vol. XII (Albany), Basically Baker with the Buselli/Wallarab Jazz Orchestra (Patois), and Sky Scrapings: Saxophone Music of Don Freund (AUR). Walsh has appeared at conferences of the International Association for Jazz Education, Jazz Education Network, North American Saxophone Alliance, and World Saxophone Congress. He is a Yamaha Performing Artist and a Vandoren Artist. He has taught at the Jamey Aebersold Summer Jazz Workshops since 1991. He co-leads the IU Summer Saxophone Academy with Otis Murphy and is co-director of the College Audition Preparation Workshop. Walsh earned degrees in Saxophone Performance and Jazz Studies from Indiana University, where his principal teachers were distinguished classical saxophonist Eugene Rousseau and renowned jazz educator David Baker. His other influential teachers include Mike Tracy, Pat LaBarbera, Jerry Coker, and David Liebman.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
location: LILLY LIBRARY - Room Number: Ball Room
description: "Myths are the world’s dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

location: GLOBAL & INTERNATIONAL STUDIES BUILDING - Room Number: 2134
description: New Immigrants and Multilingual Linguistic Landscape in Taiwan by Ching-Yu Na and Serafín M. Coronel-Molina explores how migration reshapes language use and public signage in Taiwan. Through ethnographic and geosemiotic perspectives, the book examines multilingual practices, identity, and social inclusion, highlighting the linguistic presence and contributions of new immigrant communities within Taiwan's evolving sociolinguistic landscape.Ching-Yu Na is an English teacher and curriculum coordinator at a public elementary school in Taoyuan City, Taiwan, and has also taught at the university level. Her research interests include sociolinguistics, ethnographic and geosemiotic perspectives on multilingual linguistic landscapes, TESOL, and World Englishes.Serafín M. Coronel-Molina is Professor in the Literacy, Culture, and Language Education and International and Comparative Education programs in the Department of Curriculum and Instruction at the School of Education. His research focuses on sociolinguistics, language policy, planning, and revitalization, as well as ethnographic and geosemiotic approaches to multilingual linguistic landscapes, and translingual and translanguaging practices in education.

title: Teenage Wasteland | Additional Films and Guests
location: IU Cinema,1213 East 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47406, USA
description: At first glance, there’s nothing especially memorable about Middletown, N.Y. Despite being one of the largest cities in Orange County, and only 70 miles north of Manhattan, most New Yorkers have never heard of it. According to former student Mike Regan, “You were always going somewhere else—going to the city, going to the Jersey Shore or going to Long Island, and everybody was always trying to get out.” In the early '90s, a group of high-school students—with encouragement from an unconventional English teacher—decided to take a deeper look at their seemingly unmemorable town to produce an investigative documentary. Banding together to confront indifferent adults, corrupt politicians, and a violent criminal organization threatening their small town, what they uncovered sent shockwaves throughout their community. Teenage Wasteland is a coming-of-age story based on exclusive access to hundreds of hours of candid, humorous, and nostalgic video outtakes, and the cooperation of Fred Isseks and his intrepid students as they reckon, 30 years later, with a defining event in their lives and a remarkable story of civic courage. title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
location: LILLY LIBRARY - Room Number: Ball Room
description: "Myths are the world’s dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

location: The Ostrom Workshop, 513 N PARK AVE - Room Number: Tocqueville
description: Bio  Adriana is an Amazonian environmental anthropologist focusing on resource management, traditional communities, conservation, gender equity, development, and socioenvironmental challenges in the Brazilian Amazon. She holds a B.A. in Social Sciences and an M.A. in Sociology & Anthropology from the University of Pará, Brazil. Over the past decade, she has been involved in researching socioenvironmental conflicts, development, and the resistance of rural communities in Amazonia as an activist-scholar. Adriana was previously a grantee of the Amazon Rainforest Fund, contributing to the journalist collaborative project "Quilombolas, Invisible Protectors of the Forest, in Sight of COVID-19" https://pulitzercenter.org/projects/quilombolas-invisble-protectors-forest-sight-covid-19-portuguese (https://nam12.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpulitzercenter.org%2Fprojects%2Fquilombolas-invisble-protectors-forest-sight-covid-19-portuguese&data=05%7C02%7Cmackka%40iu.edu%7Ccd4eb2a425784381849508ddd389bf51%7C1113be34aed14d00ab4bcdd02510be91%7C1%7C0%7C638899310768561227%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=OEEE0nioleIGY2XjOsqO%2BNCZcPMfqzT%2B%2FXhDn5n52Bs%3D&reserved=0). Currently pursuing her Ph.D. in Anthropology at Indiana University, Adriana's research focuses on the intersection of formal rules and social norms in the arapaima fisheries community-based management. She is part of the project "Integrating Cross-scale Socio-Ecological Feedbacks in Freshwater Fisheries" co-led by Professor Eduardo Brondizio and is a member of the Center for Analysis of Socio-Ecological Landscapes (CASEL) at Indiana University.About the Ostrom Workshop Research Series  Learn about innovative research by Graduate Students and Visiting Scholars as they advance the mission of the Ostrom Workshop, building upon the theme of governance to understand and address major societal problems. title: Ostrom Workshop | Research Series: Paulo Ramos
location: The Ostrom Workshop, 513 N PARK AVE - Room Number: Tocqueville
description: Bio  Paulo Ramos is born from the womb of his mother, Terezinha Ramos de Jesus. He is an Afro-Brazilian visual artist, performer, actor, and poet whose multidisciplinarywork spans video, performance, and poetry. His acclaimed poetry book, Corpos d'água, was published in 2023 in Brazil. And in 2026, the book, titled Bodies of Water, will be released in the United States, in English, by NP-PRESS and Counterpath Press. Ramos' compelling performance piece, presented at the 12th At First Sigh New Works Festival Indiana University and in venues across São Paulo and Tepoztlán, gave rise to the thought-provoking videoperformance Bodies of Water: Threebuckets: a river, a mangrow, and a sean. Paulo Ramos is a Ph.D. in Social Science in Gender and Black Studies in PUCSP. Pontifícia Universidade Católica de São Paulo,Paulo Ramos continues to explore and amplify the narratives of Afro-Brazilian identity.Abstract  Bodies of Water is an artistic performance, an academic confrontation grounded in the studies of Denise Ferreira da Silva (2020), constructed through a poetic pathway in which the body becomes theoretical expansion. According to Denise Ferreira da Silva, anticolonial art must be a confrontation.  Bodies of Water: A Hybrid Cartography Flowing into an etnographyWE is part of my doctoral research, built from the memory, orality, and ancestry of Black women who turn their daily notes into the reinvention of life in community. This reinvention constitutes their intellectual production, naming everything that inhabits space or emerges from the ways they experience the world—one that is crossed by race, class, and the environmental. It concerns the relationship between water and Black women-mothers as a way of thinking existence, both as a site of escape and of resistance.  Here, I propose to reflect from a fieldwork perspective that traverses my own self—not through an autoethnographic method, but immersed in an etnographyWE, a new theory in development for thinking about the women and the waters that came before me.  Thus, Bodies of Water brings forth tension, discomfort, and a critiCREATIVE approach developed alongside my research on my grandmother, my mother, my aunt, and the waters—and on environmental racism (Costa 2022; Pacheco 2012). Bodies of Water is body–time–space poetry. Above all, it is confrontation. It is a profound dialogue between the Black body and water—living elements, yet constrained by the violence imposed by temporality.  Ancestrality and Afropessimism are both present here, navigating together in the same vessel through the currents of the Black body (Pinho 2021; Smith 2015); between these two concepts, ecology emerges as the missing link that connects them.About the Ostrom Workshop Research Series  Learn about innovative research by Graduate Students and Visiting Scholars as they advance the mission of the Ostrom Workshop, building upon the theme of governance to understand and address major societal problems. title: A Conversation with Boots Riley | Additional Films and Guests
location: Fine Arts Building, Room 102,1201 East 7th Street, Bloomington, IN 47405, USA
description:
Enigmatic director (and activist, screenwriter, producer, poet, rapper, and speaker) Boots Riley is returning to IU for a wide-ranging conversation on all things, art, advocacy, and his new film I Love Boosters.

Riley's directorial debut Sorry to Bother You premiered to strong critical acclaim at the Sundance Film Festival. By embedding messages regarding economic and class critique as well as politically progressive movement building into dystopian science-fiction satire, Sorry to Bother You brought issues surrounding income inequality into wide public discussion in the United States and abroad. His seven-part series I’m a Virgo released in summer 2023 to critical acclaim. The absurdist comedy about a 13-foot-tall Black man who lives in Oakland, California stars Jharrel Jerome (who won an Emmy for his role in Ava DuVernay’s When They See Us), Brett Gray, Walton Goggins, Mike Epps, Carmen Ejogo, Kara Young, Olivia Washington, and Allius Barnes with a score by Tuneyards. Riley is also the founding member and lead vocalist of The Coup and Street Sweeper Social Club featuring Tom Morello of Rage Against The Machine on guitar.

His new movie, I Love Boosters, premiered at SXSW on March 12 as the festival's opening film, and will screen as a free sneak preview (with Riley in attendance) at IU Cinema on April 8 at 7pm https://cinema.indiana.edu/upcoming-films/screening/2026-spring-wednesday-april-8-700pm .

Riley will be in conversation with WFIU's own Alex Chambers. Chambers is a producer at WFIU, where he produces and co-hosts Nice Work, a weekly podcast and radio show, and created the podcast Inner States. He co-produced How to Survive the Future for Indiana Humanities, along with other podcasts and radio stories. He teaches podcasting at the Indiana University Media School.

title: Wiles Lecture: "A Rebellious Generation: Solidarity Activism in Poland and the Diaspora" with Mary Erdmans
location: Indiana Memorial Union - Room Number: Federal Room
description: This talk looks at activism among political refugees from the Solidarność movement. The social-historical context created a political generation and radical disposition that impelled activism over time and space. Factors that explain activism in the diaspora include biographical availability, geographic location, and transnational political networks.  Mary Erdmans is Professor of Sociology at Case Western Reserve University. A Fulbright Scholar and past president of the Polish American Historical Association, she authored three award-winning books: Opposite Poles, The Grasinski Girls, and On Becoming a Teen Mom. Her articles have appeared in Sociological Quarterly, Journal of American Ethnic History, and Studia Migracynjne.Reception to follow.Sponsored by the Polish Studies Center with additional support from The Byrnes Institute (REEI), the Department of Slavic and East European Languages and Cultures, the Department of Sociology, and the Institute for European Studies.

The intent behind this movie night is to spread awareness about the difficulties of seasons and changes in life. title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
location: LILLY LIBRARY - Room Number: Ball Room
description: "Myths are the world’s dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.
